name: Islam
summary: Islam, as the Qur'an and the reference works present it, is a revealed monotheistic religion whose law (the sharia) is a divinely ordained code for private and public life, with an Islamic law and state rather than a separation of religion and politics. It prescribes fixed penalties for some crimes, forbids interest, makes charity and zakah obligatory, permits polygyny up to four wives, and allows fighting against aggressors, with classical jurists also permitting wars of expansion.
scope: Islam as a whole religion, as defined by Britannica's entries on Islam, the sharia, jihad and ribā and by the Qur'an itself. Positions of later movements (Islamism, Salafi-jihadism, Islamic modernism, Islamic feminism, Islamic socialism) are separate subjects and are not used. Where the Qur'an and the jurists differ, the answer is a split or null.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Britannica says the sharia regulates marriage, divorce and inheritance as family law, and the Qur'an (4:3, 24:2) regulates marriage and sexual relations.

animal-use-humane.rationale: The Qur'an (16:5, 5:1) says livestock were created for people and are lawful food.

armed-resistance-to-occupation.rationale: The Qur'an (22:39) gives permission to fight to those who are fought because they were wronged, and Britannica says modern Muslim thinkers restrict fighting to self-defence against aggression.

assisted-dying.rationale: The Qur'an (4:29) forbids Muslims to kill themselves or one another, which excludes helping someone end their life.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: The Qur'an (5:1, 6:142, 16:5) declares grazing livestock lawful to eat and made for people, so banning their slaughter contradicts it.

ban-interest.rationale: The Qur'an (2:275) says Allah has forbidden interest, and Britannica reports that the sharia precludes any form of interest on a loan, with some Muslim states making it illegal.

civilians-legitimate-targets.rationale: The Qur'an (2:190) restricts fighting to those who fight the believers and forbids transgression.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: The Qur'an (102:1) says competition in worldly increase diverts people from what matters.

death-penalty.rationale: The Qur'an prescribes retribution for murder (2:178, 5:45) and death or crucifixion for those who wage war and spread corruption (5:33); Britannica notes fixed punishments (hadd) in the sharia.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: The Qur'an (2:190, 22:39) commands fighting those who fight the believers, and Britannica says jihad includes fighting in self-defence against aggressors.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: The Qur'an (12:40) states that legislation belongs to Allah alone, and Britannica describes the law as the expression of the divine will.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Britannica says Islamic rule combined egalitarianism within the community of the faithful with official discrimination against followers of other religions, who paid the jizyah (Qur'an 9:29).

filial-duty.rationale: The Qur'an (17:23) decrees good treatment of parents, including when one or both reach old age with the believer.

humans-entitled-to-use-animals.rationale: The Qur'an (16:5) says the grazing livestock were created for people, who draw warmth and benefit from them and eat them.

initiating-nondefensive-force-unjustifie.rationale: Britannica reports classical jurists permitting wars of expansion, and also that the Qur'an forbids initiating war and allows fighting only against aggressors.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: The Qur'an restricts marriage across religions: believers may not marry polytheists (2:221) and believing women are not lawful wives for disbelievers (60:10), while chaste women of the Scripture are permitted (5:5).

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Britannica describes the sharia as God's law drawn from the Qur'an and the Sunnah, and the Qur'an (5:44-45) condemns those who do not judge by what Allah has revealed.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: The Qur'an (24:2) prescribes lashes for extramarital sexual intercourse by unmarried men and women, so legal sex work between consenting adults contradicts it.

military-force-beyond-defence.rationale: Britannica reports classical jurists permitting wars of expansion, and also that the Qur'an forbids initiating war and allows fighting only against aggressors.

military-force-for-human-rights.rationale: The Qur'an (4:75) calls on believers to fight for the oppressed who cry out for deliverance.

more-religion-public.rationale: Britannica says Islam unites the spiritual and temporal and regulates social as well as individual life, with an Islamic law and state; the Qur'an (22:41) says rulers given authority establish prayer and zakah and enjoin what is right.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: The Qur'an (2:190, 22:39) permits fighting those who fight the believers, and Britannica says jihad includes self-defence.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: The Qur'an (2:177) counts giving wealth to relatives, orphans and the needy as righteousness, and (9:60) makes zakah an obligation imposed by Allah.

one-spouse-at-a-time.rationale: The Qur'an (4:3) permits a man to marry two, three or four women, provided he is just.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: The Qur'an (17:31) tells people not to kill their children for fear of poverty, because Allah provides for them and for their parents.

premarital-sex.rationale: The Qur'an (24:2) prescribes a hundred lashes for the unmarried man or woman found guilty of sexual intercourse.

racial-pride.rationale: The Qur'an (49:13) says peoples and tribes were made so that they may know one another and that the most noble is the most righteous.

religion-from-peoples-character.rationale: The Qur'an (42:13, 10:47) presents religion as ordained by God and brought by a messenger to every nation, not grown from a people's character.

religion-illusion.rationale: Britannica presents Islam as God's revealed command and the Qur'an (3:19, 4:82) presents its message as true, so calling religion an illusion contradicts it.

religious-nation.rationale: Britannica says the community-state of Islam emerged at Medina as a community bound by a common faith, and that all Muslim segments share a sense of belonging to a single community (ummah).

religious-offensive-war.rationale: Britannica reports classical jurists permitting wars of expansion to extend Muslim rule, and also that the Qur'an forbids initiating war and allows fighting only against aggressors.

resist-oppression-despite-death.rationale: The Qur'an (4:75) asks why believers do not fight for the oppressed men, women and children who cry out for deliverance.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: The Qur'an calls itself a Book about which there is no doubt (2:2) and says it would contain much contradiction had it come from other than Allah (4:82).

separate-church-state.rationale: Britannica says Islam unites religion and the temporal sphere, with an Islamic law and state, and that separating them is a 20th-century view of some Muslim thinkers.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: The Qur'an (4:34) says men are in charge of women, which contradicts equal authority between spouses.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The Qur'an (4:59) tells believers to refer disputes to Allah and the Messenger even in dealing with those in authority, and (5:44-45) condemns judging by anything other than what Allah revealed.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: The Qur'an (12:40, 3:19) holds that Allah alone is to be worshipped and that the religion with Allah is Islam, which excludes state promotion of atheism.

state-supports-good-ways-of-life.rationale: The Qur'an (22:41, 3:104) says rulers given authority and the community enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.

taxation-theft.rationale: Britannica reports that Islamic law mandates zakah (tithe) and ushr (land tax), and the Qur'an (9:60) makes zakah an obligation with officials employed to collect it.

notes: Researched by theme: economy (interest, zakah), government and law (sharia, authority), society and family (marriage, sexual morality, parents), liberty (punishments), world and war (jihad), ecology (animals). Most statements are null because the Qur'an and the reference works record no stated position on them, or the jurists and modern Muslim thinkers differ and no source speaks for Islam as a whole. Hadith collections were not used.
